why: The drone always takes the cheaper way round the ring between consecutive requests, so the task is many 'cost of an arc' queries. A prefix sum over transitionTime answers each arc (clockwise or counter-clockwise) in O(1).
hints: Between two consecutive requests there are only two possible routes around the ring. What do you need to compute their costs quickly?

Leaving hub i costs transitionTime[i] whichever way you go. The clockwise cost from a to b is a sum of a contiguous (possibly wrapping) block of transitionTime, and so is the counter-clockwise cost: prefix sums give both in O(1).
Build pfx over the 1-based transitionTime, keep the current hub (start 1), and for each request add min(clockwise, counter) then move there. O(m + n), 64-bit totals.
pitfalls: The cost is paid by the hub you leave, not by an edge between two hubs: going counter-clockwise from hub 1 to hub m costs transitionTime[1].
Consecutive identical requests (and a first request of hub 1) cost 0.
Wrap-around arcs need total - (inner block); off-by-one errors in the prefix indices are the usual bug.
statement:
There are m hubs numbered 1..m on a ring (hub m is next to hub 1). From hub i the drone can fly to either neighbour, and leaving hub i costs transitionTime[i] (1-based) whichever direction it goes.

The drone starts at hub 1 and must visit requestedHubs[0], requestedHubs[1], … in order. Return the minimum total travel time.

Worked example. transitionTime = [3, 2, 1], requestedHubs = [1, 3, 3, 2].

  • Hub 1 to hub 1: already there, 0.
  • Hub 1 to hub 3: clockwise 1→2→3 costs tt[1] + tt[2] = 3 + 2 = 5; counter-clockwise 1→3 costs tt[1] = 3. Take 3.
  • Hub 3 to hub 3: 0.
  • Hub 3 to hub 2: counter-clockwise 3→2 costs tt[3] = 1; clockwise 3→1→2 costs tt[3] + tt[1] = 4. Take 1.
  • Total: 0 + 3 + 0 + 1 = 4.
constraints:
• Numeric bounds are not stated in the source. Reasonable: 1 <= m, n <= 10^5, 1 <= transitionTime[i] <= 10^9, 1 <= requestedHubs[j] <= m
  • The answer may exceed 32 bits (return a long).
